labEmbed.title: α 粒子散射 · 实验台

dialogue.speaker: 华生
dialogue.text: Manchester, Coupland Street, nineteen-nine. In the dark room Geiger and Marsden are counting flashes on a zinc-sulphide screen. Most of the α-particles from the source go nearly straight through the thin foil — the scene looks quieter than it is.

claim.citation: H. Geiger & E. Marsden, Proc. R. Soc. A 82 (1909) 495–500
claim.notes: cite fact-gm1909-paper / fact-gm1909-zns-method / fact-gm1909-forward-majority. Name Geiger & Marsden's labour; they do not speak.

dialogue.speaker: 卢瑟福
dialogue.text: But a few are turned through large angles — some even come back toward the source. They call that diffuse reflection. The scintillations on the screen are counted one by one by Geiger and Marsden; my part is to give an account of what those counts mean. Early on, people slighted the α-rays because they barely penetrate — the more we measure, the less we can treat them as a trifle.

claim.citation: H. Geiger & E. Marsden, Proc. R. Soc. A 82 (1909) 495–500
claim.notes: cite fact-gm1909-diffuse-reflection. Credit counting; no ledger slang.

dialogue.speaker: 卢瑟福
dialogue.text: Take it as a working hypothesis for now: the positive electricity nearly gathered in a very small region at the centre of the atom — a concentrated central charge. Most paths barely deflect; a few deflect violently. That looks more like striking a strong local field than piling up weak turns inside a diffuse sphere of positive electricity. The evidence is still lengthening; until we have a more decisive proof, I will not speak as if the case were closed.

claim.notes: cite fact-ruth1911-central-charge. Period term central charge; no nucleus banner. Working-hypothesis register for 1909 scene.

dialogue.speaker: 华生
dialogue.text: Later storytellers love the picture of a fifteen-inch shell striking tissue paper and bouncing back. It sounds fine — but that is late recollection, not a line from the nineteen-nine dark-room notebooks. We should not live on legends. Shall we try it ourselves at the apparatus?

dialogue.speaker: 旁白
dialogue.text: Textbooks later call this the nuclear model of the atom: nearly all the mass and positive charge packed into a tiny centre, with electrons outside. In the laboratory of this period one more often said central charge. Either way, a plum-pudding picture with positive electricity smeared through the whole atomic volume cannot account for these rare but stubborn large-angle deflections.

claim.citation: 人教版选必三 第四§3–§4（教材用语：核式结构）
claim.notes: Textbook register; nuclear model wording OK here only. Align era-op-nucleus-word-anachronism.

dialogue.speaker: 华生
dialogue.text: At night I read the day's scintillation counts again. Most paths nearly forward, a few at large angles — the diffuse positive sphere of the plum-pudding picture never seems to pile up so violent a deflection. The central-charge sketch, though, can make sense of those sharp flashes on the screen. The dull numbers from daylight start to bite after dark.

dialogue.speaker: 卢瑟福
dialogue.text: Large angles are scarce — everyone grants that — yet they are not zero. Geiger and Marsden put those rare flashes into the notebook; they are not there for ornament. If the positive charge is truly concentrated at the centre, those rare large-angle paths can stand; if we cling to a diffuse sphere plus compound scattering alone, the returning paths become a nuisance. I want an account that will bear the apparatus and the foil thickness — not a neat slogan.

claim.citation: Lodge night review — aligned to fact-gm1909-diffuse-reflection + fact-ruth1911-central-charge

dialogue.speaker: 旁白
dialogue.text: In the lodge we first keep what was seen apart from what is guessed: observation here, hypothesis there. Tomorrow, back in the laboratory — change the foil thickness, watch whether the angular pattern shifts. Asking the apparatus again beats arguing under the lamp.
